items.readable_text:
Content:
In the earlier topics, we saw that symmetry can force many Fourier coefficients to be zero automatically.
In particular, if a [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic function is even, then its Fourier series has cosine terms only.

Content:
A Fourier cosine series uses this idea when a function is initially given only on the half-interval [MATH: [0,\pi),] but we want a full Fourier series on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)] (and then a [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension to all real [MATH: x]).

Content:
To do this, we start with a function [MATH: F(x)] on [MATH: [0,\pi)] and define its even extension [MATH: f(x)] to [MATH: (-\pi,\pi)] by
[MATH: {F(x),|x ∈ [0, π),; F(− x),|x ∈ (− π, 0).]

Content:
For example, a function [MATH: F(x),] defined on [MATH: x \in [0,1),] and its even extension [MATH: f(x)] to [MATH: x \in (-1,1)] are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a60be008a552f0c8de9c07a97fc1b3be]

Content:
By construction, [MATH: f] is an even function, meaning [MATH: f(-x)=f(x)]. Because [MATH: f] is even, its Fourier series on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)] has cosine terms only:
[MATH: f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos(nx)]

Content:
Since [MATH: f(x)] is even and [MATH: \cos(nx)] is even for any [MATH: n\ge 1,] the product [MATH: f(x)\cos(nx)] is even too. Therefore, the cosine coefficients can be computed using the half-range formulas:
[MATH: a_{0}|= (1)/(π)∫_{− π}^{π}f(x)dx; = (1)/(π) ⋅ 2∫_{0}^{π}f(x)dx; = (2)/(π)∫_{0}^{π}f(x)dx,]
and for [MATH: n\ge 1,]
[MATH: a_{n}|= (1)/(π)∫_{− π}^{π}f(x)\cos (nx)dx; = (1)/(π) ⋅ 2∫_{0}^{π}f(x)\cos (nx)dx; = (2)/(π)∫_{0}^{π}f(x)\cos (nx)dx.]

Content:
So in practice, the workflow is the following:

Content:
1. Start with [MATH: F] on [MATH: [0,\pi)] and form the even extension [MATH: f] on [MATH: (-\pi,\pi).]
2. Compute [MATH: a_0] and [MATH: a_n] from the half-range integrals on [MATH: [0,\pi).]
3. Write the Fourier cosine series of [MATH: f.]

Content:
Let's see some concrete examples.

For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by [MATH: a_0=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\,\text{d}x.]

In our case, [MATH: f(x)=\sin\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}\right)] for [MATH: x \in (0,\pi).] So, substituting into the formula, we get [MATH: a_{0}|= (2)/(π)∫_{0}^{π}\sin ((3x)/(4))dx; = (2)/(π)[− (4)/(3)\cos ((3x)/(4))]_{0}^{π}; = − (8)/(3π)(\cos ((3π)/(4)) − \cos (0)); = − (8)/(3π)(− (sqrt(2))/(2) − 1); = 4 3 π (2 + 2).]

items.title: Computing the Cosine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: F(x)=-6x-2] for [MATH: x\in[0,\pi).] Find the missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the even [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of the function [MATH: F(x).]

[MATH: XX_{X}^{X}]
sections.readable_text:
Let [MATH: F(x)=-6x-2] for [MATH: x\in[0,\pi).] Find the missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the even [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of the function [MATH: F(x).]

[MATH: XX_{X}^{X}]

sections.normalized_html:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by [MATH: a_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\cos(nx)\,\text{d}x.]

In our case, [MATH: f(x)=-6x-2] for [MATH: x \in (0,\pi).] So, substituting into the formula, we get [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi (-6x-2) \cos(nx)\,\text{d}x.]

We use the integration by parts: [MATH: u = − 6x − 2|⇒u^{′} = − 6; v^{′} = \cos (nx)|⇒v = (1)/(n)\sin (nx)]

Thus, we obtain [MATH: a_{n}|= (2)/(π)(uv|_{0}^{π} − ∫_{0}^{π}vu^{′}dx); = (2)/(π)((1)/(n)[(− 6x − 2)\sin (nx)]_{0}^{π} + (6)/(n)∫_{0}^{π}\sin (nx)dx); = (2)/(nπ)(((− 6π − 2)\sin (nπ) + 2\sin (0)) − (6)/(n)[\cos (nx)]_{0}^{π}); = (2)/(nπ)(0 − (6)/(n)(\cos (nπ) − \cos (0))); = (12(1 − \cos (nπ)))/(n^{2}π).]

Therefore, since [MATH: \cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,] we have [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{12(1-(-1)^n)}{\pi n^2}.]

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is [MATH: f(x) \sim (-2-3\pi) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{12(1-(-1)^n)}{\pi n^2}} \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\cos(nx)}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In the earlier topics, we saw that symmetry can force many Fourier coefficients to be zero automatically.
In particular, if a [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic function is even, then its Fourier series has cosine terms only.

Content:
A Fourier cosine series uses this idea when a function is initially given only on the half-interval [MATH: [0,\pi),] but we want a full Fourier series on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)] (and then a [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension to all real [MATH: x]).

Content:
To do this, we start with a function [MATH: F(x)] on [MATH: [0,\pi)] and define its even extension [MATH: f(x)] to [MATH: (-\pi,\pi)] by
[MATH: {F(x),|x ∈ [0, π),; F(− x),|x ∈ (− π, 0).]

Content:
For example, a function [MATH: F(x),] defined on [MATH: x \in [0,1),] and its even extension [MATH: f(x)] to [MATH: x \in (-1,1)] are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a60be008a552f0c8de9c07a97fc1b3be]

Content:
By construction, [MATH: f] is an even function, meaning [MATH: f(-x)=f(x)]. Because [MATH: f] is even, its Fourier series on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)] has cosine terms only:
[MATH: f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos(nx)]

Content:
Since [MATH: f(x)] is even and [MATH: \cos(nx)] is even for any [MATH: n\ge 1,] the product [MATH: f(x)\cos(nx)] is even too. Therefore, the cosine coefficients can be computed using the half-range formulas:
[MATH: a_{0}|= (1)/(π)∫_{− π}^{π}f(x)dx; = (1)/(π) ⋅ 2∫_{0}^{π}f(x)dx; = (2)/(π)∫_{0}^{π}f(x)dx,]
and for [MATH: n\ge 1,]
[MATH: a_{n}|= (1)/(π)∫_{− π}^{π}f(x)\cos (nx)dx; = (1)/(π) ⋅ 2∫_{0}^{π}f(x)\cos (nx)dx; = (2)/(π)∫_{0}^{π}f(x)\cos (nx)dx.]

Content:
So in practice, the workflow is the following:

Content:
1. Start with [MATH: F] on [MATH: [0,\pi)] and form the even extension [MATH: f] on [MATH: (-\pi,\pi).]
2. Compute [MATH: a_0] and [MATH: a_n] from the half-range integrals on [MATH: [0,\pi).]
3. Write the Fourier cosine series of [MATH: f.]

Content:
Let's see some concrete examples.

---

Item 2 — Example: Understanding the Even Extension of a Function

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: F(x)=x^3 - x + 5\cos x] for [MATH: x\in[0,\pi),] and let [MATH: f(x)] be the even extension of [MATH: F(x)] to [MATH: x \in (-\pi,\pi).] What is [MATH: f(x)] for [MATH: x\in(-\pi,0)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If [MATH: F(x)] is defined on [MATH: x\in[0,\pi),] the even extension of [MATH: F] is the function [MATH: f] such that
[MATH: {F(x),|x ∈ [0, π),; F(− x),|x ∈ (− π, 0).]

In our cases, for [MATH: x\in(-\pi,0),] we get
[MATH: f(x)|= F(− x); = (− x)^{3} − (− x) + 5\cos (− x); = − x^{3} + x + 5\cos x.]

Item 5 — Example: Computing the Constant Term From the Half-Range Formula

Example Prompt:
[MATH: f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \cos(nx)]
Let [MATH: F(x)=\sin\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}\right)] for [MATH: x\in[0,\pi).] The Fourier cosine series of the even [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: F(x)] is shown above. Find the expression for [MATH: a_0.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by
[MATH: a_0=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\,\text{d}x.]

In our case, [MATH: f(x)=\sin\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}\right)] for [MATH: x \in (0,\pi).] So, substituting into the formula, we get
[MATH: a_{0}|= (2)/(π)∫_{0}^{π}\sin ((3x)/(4))dx; = (2)/(π)[− (4)/(3)\cos ((3x)/(4))]_{0}^{π}; = − (8)/(3π)(\cos ((3π)/(4)) − \cos (0)); = − (8)/(3π)(− (sqrt(2))/(2) − 1); = 4 3 π (2 + 2).]

Item 8 — Example: Computing the Cosine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: F(x)=-6x-2] for [MATH: x\in[0,\pi).] Find the missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the even [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x)] of the function [MATH: F(x).]

[MATH: XX_{X}^{X}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by
[MATH: a_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\cos(nx)\,\text{d}x.]

In our case, [MATH: f(x)=-6x-2] for [MATH: x \in (0,\pi).] So, substituting into the formula, we get
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi (-6x-2) \cos(nx)\,\text{d}x.]

We use the integration by parts:
[MATH: u = − 6x − 2|⇒u^{′} = − 6; v^{′} = \cos (nx)|⇒v = (1)/(n)\sin (nx)]

Thus, we obtain
[MATH: a_{n}|= (2)/(π)(uv|_{0}^{π} − ∫_{0}^{π}vu^{′}dx); = (2)/(π)((1)/(n)[(− 6x − 2)\sin (nx)]_{0}^{π} + (6)/(n)∫_{0}^{π}\sin (nx)dx); = (2)/(nπ)(((− 6π − 2)\sin (nπ) + 2\sin (0)) − (6)/(n)[\cos (nx)]_{0}^{π}); = (2)/(nπ)(0 − (6)/(n)(\cos (nπ) − \cos (0))); = (12(1 − \cos (nπ)))/(n^{2}π).]

Therefore, since [MATH: \cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,] we have
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{12(1-(-1)^n)}{\pi n^2}.]

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is
[MATH: f(x) \sim (-2-3\pi) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty
\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{12(1-(-1)^n)}{\pi n^2}}
\cdot
\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\cos(nx)}.]
